pages.title: Introduction to Greedy Algorithms
pages.content:
Greedy algorithms is a type of algorithm, where you try to take the best option at every step, and it ends up giving the best solution in the long run as well.

Let's imagine that we are in a rectangular maze where we are starting from the bottom-left corner and we know that the exit is at the top-right. So one approach that we might try, is that at every step, we try to go up, and if that is not possible, we try to go right. 

This is a 'greedy' choice, where we are choosing what seems to be locally the best choice, but actually, the path which goes up might end in a dead end, and we actually need to take a longer path which starts out by going left! But when we talk about greedy algorithms, we are talking about problems where we know (rather we have proven), that such things don't happen. And we are sure that taking the locally best option does indeed lead to the correct optimal solution.

So, as you might have guessed, implementing a greedy solution is often easy. The hard part lies in figuring out when and where you can apply a greedy solution. And that typically involves us trying to prove that a greedy solution works, which can be hard some times.

So let us dive into the world of greedy algorithms!

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Basics of Greedy, and proofs: focus on the greedy invariant, the local choice, and why that choice preserves an optimal solution.

checkpoint.question: Why does a greedy algorithm need more than a locally best choice?
options: A proof or exchange argument must show the local choice can be part of some optimal global solution.
Greedy algorithms are correct whenever the input is already sorted.
A locally best choice is always globally optimal for every problem.
Greedy algorithms never require edge-case analysis.
checkpoint.explanation: Greedy design requires a correctness argument; convenience of implementation alone is not enough.

pages.title: Max Boy-Girl Pairs
pages.content:
You have a row of students, each either a girl ('x') or a boy ('y'). Students standing next to each other are friends. You need to form as many dance pairs as possible, where each pair consists of one boy and one girl who are friends. Each student can only be in one pair.

**Example 1:**\
Input: xy\
Students: Girl ('x') and Boy ('y') standing next to each other.\
Possible pairs: (Girl, Boy)\
Output: 1 (only one pair can be formed)


**Example 2:**\
Input: xyxxy\
Students: Girl ('x'), Boy ('y'), Girl ('x'), Girl ('x'), Boy ('y')\
Possible pairs: (Girl 1, Boy 2) and (Girl 4, Boy 5)\
Or (Boy 2, Girl 3) and (Girl 4, Boy 5)\
Output: 2 (two pairs can be formed)

**Example 3:**\
Input: yy\
Students: Boy ('y') and Boy ('y')\
Possible pairs: None (no girls to pair with)\
Output: 0


The goal is to find the maximum number of such pairs for any given string of students.**

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Basics of Greedy, and proofs: focus on the greedy invariant, the local choice, and why that choice preserves an optimal solution.

topics.title: Chopsticks
topics.description: Understand Chopsticks and practice the greedy strategy, edge cases, and correctness reasoning.

pages.title: Chopsticks
pages.content:
The chopsticks problem is a classic greedy pairing exercise. Given stick lengths and a maximum allowed difference D, we want the largest possible number of disjoint pairs.

Sort the lengths. Consider the two smallest remaining sticks: they are the closest possible pair involving the smallest stick. If their difference is at most D, pairing them is safe for maximizing the number of pairs; otherwise the smallest stick cannot pair with any later stick, so discard it and continue.

This is a typical exchange-argument pattern: sorting exposes a locally safe choice that can be committed without reducing the optimum.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Chopsticks: focus on the greedy invariant, the local choice, and why that choice preserves an optimal solution.

checkpoint.question: Why is sorting useful for the chopsticks pairing strategy?
options: It exposes the smallest adjacent gap, allowing a locally valid adjacent pair to be selected safely.
It guarantees every pair has equal-length sticks.
It removes the need to check the difference threshold.
It forces every stick to be paired.
checkpoint.explanation: After sorting, adjacent lengths are the closest candidates, which supports the greedy pairing proof.

pages.content: Suppose D = 10. And the smallest stick has a length of 20, and the second smallest stick has a length of 40. What can we deduce from this?

topics.title: Evacuate to Moon
topics.description: Understand Evacuate to Moon and practice the greedy strategy, edge cases, and correctness reasoning.

pages.title: EVacuate to Moon
pages.content:
This lesson uses a greedy matching pattern. When two sorted collections must be matched and the contribution of a pair is determined by the smaller member, aligning the capacities in sorted order preserves the maximum possible total contribution.

The important idea is not the story but the ordering: sort the two collections, match corresponding positions, and reason about why crossing two matches cannot improve the total. This is a useful technique whenever a pair contribution is monotone in its smaller endpoint.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Evacuate to Moon: focus on the greedy invariant, the local choice, and why that choice preserves an optimal solution.

checkpoint.question: Why can sorted matching support the greedy energy-allocation strategy?
options: Pairing capacities in sorted order preserves the best attainable contribution from the smaller side of each pair.
Sorting makes every car receive its largest possible outlet.
Sorting allows capacities to be ignored.
The order of pairing can never affect an optimization problem.
checkpoint.explanation: The sorted matching aligns capacities so the sum of pairwise minima is maximized.

pages.title: Snakes, Mongooses and the Ultimate Election
pages.content:
In this election problem, snakes and mongooses are arranged in a row. A mongoose may eat at most one neighboring snake before the vote is counted.

The greedy objective is to maximize the number of snakes removed. Each mongoose should consume an available adjacent snake, while respecting that a snake can be eaten only once. After the elimination phase, compare the remaining populations to determine the winner.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Snakes and Mongooses: focus on the greedy invariant, the local choice, and why that choice preserves an optimal solution.

checkpoint.question: What is the key greedy decision in the election problem?
options: Each mongoose should consume an available adjacent snake while respecting the one-snake-per-mongoose limit.
Every mongoose must consume both neighbors.
Only snakes may choose which neighbor is removed.
The election can be decided before any snakes are consumed.
checkpoint.explanation: The goal is to maximize snake removals under the local one-eating constraint.

pages.title: Optimal Snake Mongoose Strategy
pages.content: It's clear that the mongooses will kill as many snakes as possible. If every mongoose decides to eat some snake neighbor of it, at random, would it always be optimal? If not, in which of these cases, can it be possible that the most number of snakes isn't killed, if there isn't a clear strategy?

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Snakes and Mongooses: focus on the greedy invariant, the local choice, and why that choice preserves an optimal solution.

pages.title: Optimal Snake Elimination
pages.content: So it's clear that the mongooses should have a strategy in place, so that put together they kill the maximum number of snakes. What should that strategy be?

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Snakes and Mongooses: focus on the greedy invariant, the local choice, and why that choice preserves an optimal solution.

topics.title: Maximum Score
topics.description: Understand Maximum Score and practice the greedy strategy, edge cases, and correctness reasoning.

pages.title: Maximum Score
pages.content:
The normalized version of this lesson demonstrates a simple greedy selection principle. At each position there are two candidate values, and exactly one must be chosen.

When each position contributes independently to the final sum, the optimal local choice is simply the larger candidate. The lesson is useful because it highlights an important greedy test: before reaching for a complex global strategy, check whether decisions are independent and therefore safely optimizable one position at a time.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Maximum Score: focus on the greedy invariant, the local choice, and why that choice preserves an optimal solution.

checkpoint.question: What makes choosing the larger candidate at a position valid in this normalized maximum-score task?
options: Each position contributes independently, so taking max(A_i, B_i) maximizes that position's contribution.
The first position determines every later value.
Both candidates must be added at every position.
Sorting is mandatory before choosing a value.
checkpoint.explanation: Because the normalized task has independent choices, the total is maximized by maximizing each position.

pages.title: Maximize Disjoint Pair Sum
pages.content:
This problem combines sorting, a local feasibility test, and greedy selection. After sorting the array, inspect the largest remaining value together with its nearest smaller neighbor.

If their difference is strictly less than D, taking that pair gives the largest available contribution among feasible pairs involving the current maximum. Otherwise the current maximum cannot form a valid pair with any smaller value, so it can be skipped.

The disjointness requirement means that once a pair is selected, both elements are removed from further consideration.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Maximize Disjoint Pair Sum: focus on the greedy invariant, the local choice, and why that choice preserves an optimal solution.

checkpoint.question: Why is the largest valid adjacent pair considered first after sorting?
options: Among pairs satisfying the threshold, using the largest values gives the greatest immediate contribution while consuming only those two elements.
The largest values are always the closest.
Every pair must contain the global maximum.
Descending order eliminates the need for the threshold check.
checkpoint.explanation: Sorting makes adjacent elements natural candidates; taking the largest valid pair maximizes the pair contribution.

pages.title: Maximize Pair Sum Algorithm
pages.content:
This seems very similar to the chopsticks problem. Why can't we just reuse our solution to that problem here?

Recall that our solution there was to sort the array, start from the smallest and keep pairing adjacent elements whenever we could.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Maximize Disjoint Pair Sum: focus on the greedy invariant, the local choice, and why that choice preserves an optimal solution.

pages.title: Optimal Pairing
pages.content: We know that we are going to sort the array, and iterate from largest to smallest. What exactly should the implementation be to make the greedy choice?

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Maximize Disjoint Pair Sum: focus on the greedy invariant, the local choice, and why that choice preserves an optimal solution.
